summary: Chinese nouns do not change for number. Quantity is shown by numerals with measure words (三个洋葱), by context, or with 们 for groups of people.
traps: Never add 们 to things: *洋葱们.

notes.text: Greek marks the plural on noun, article and adjective (το βιβλίο → τα βιβλία); Chinese marks it nowhere — 书 is one book or many, and 们 is only for groups of people.
Russian marks plural and case together (книга → книги, after five книг); Chinese 书 never changes.
Spanish adds -s / -es to noun, article and adjective (los libros nuevos); Chinese adds nothing: 新书 is ‘new book’ or ‘new books’.
English adds -s even after numbers (three books); Chinese never: 三本书. 们 is not -s: it is only for people (孩子们) and never after a number.
French plural is mostly silent in speech (livre / livres) but shown by the article (le / les); Chinese shows it with neither — only context, numbers, 这些 and 很多.
German plurals are irregular (Buch → Bücher, Tisch → Tische) and learned per noun; Chinese has nothing to learn here.
Hindi marks the plural on nouns and verbs (लड़का → लड़के); Chinese marks it nowhere, except 们 for groups of people.
Persian -hā is left out after numbers (se ketāb ‘three books’); Chinese leaves the plural out always, and 们 is only for people.
Marathi plurals change the noun according to its gender class (मुलगा → मुलगे, पुस्तक → पुस्तके); Chinese nouns never change.
Arabic has sound and broken plurals (kitāb → kutub) and a dual; Chinese has neither: 书, 两本书, 三本书.
Hebrew plurals in -im / -ot (sefer → sfarim) agree with adjectives and verbs; Chinese marks no plural at all.
Turkish -lar / -ler is dropped after numbers (iki kitap ‘two book’); Chinese treats every noun like that, all the time.
Japanese also leaves nouns unmarked (本 is ‘book’ or ‘books’) and has -たち for groups of people (子供たち ~ 孩子们); the two systems are very close.
Korean -들 is optional and mostly used for people (학생들 ~ 学生们); Chinese 们 is narrower still: never on things, never after a number.
Finnish marks the plural in every case (kirja → kirjat, kirjoissa); Chinese never changes the noun.
Hungarian keeps the noun singular after numbers (három könyv ‘three book’), but has a plural -k elsewhere (könyvek); Chinese keeps the noun bare everywhere.
Swahili marks the plural with the class prefix (kitabu → vitabu, mtu → watu); Chinese has no prefixes and no plural.
Luganda marks the plural by changing the class prefix (omuntu → abantu, ekitabo → ebitabo); Chinese 人 is one person or many.
Vietnamese nouns do not change either; những / các before a noun mark plurality when needed, where Chinese uses 这些, 一些 or 很多.
Inuktitut distinguishes singular, dual and plural on the noun (inuk, inuuk, inuit); Chinese marks none of them.
